nm_spaghetti_western_wall.blurb: A mostly vertical wall in the Upper East Fork canyon of the Jemez Mountains, set a short stroll downstream of the bigger Monster Wall along the river. It holds 22 routes, almost all of them bolted, with a couple of trad lines mixed in. The grades start in the 5.7 range and run up to 5.12, with the heaviest cluster around 5.11, so it suits climbers who find the neighbouring wall too stiff. Expect an easy, scenic hike in with a few stream crossings on stones and logs, and depending on water level you may get your feet wet. Some loose rock and grit are part of the deal.

nm_east_of_eden.blurb: A compact basalt sport crag in Eden Canyon, one of the canyons of the Diablo Canyon complex outside Santa Fe, sitting on a plateau above red soft sediment. All 22 routes are bolted, with face climbing mixed with a few crack sections, and nearly everything falls between 5.10 and 5.13. Most lines are 5.11 and 5.12, so this is a place for stronger sport climbers rather than beginners. The wall faces northwest and stays shaded well into the afternoon, which makes it a good choice when the weather is hot. The base is reached by the same hike used for the main Eden wall, heading up the east side of the wide arroyo.

nm_spook_main_wall.blurb: The principal wall of Spook Canyon, one of the Box climbing areas a few miles west of Socorro. The routes are short, roughly 40 to 50 feet, and mostly bolted, with a handful of trad lines and one boulder problem; the beginner end starts around 5.7 and the top end reaches the low 5.13s, with a decent number of 5.9s and a spread of 5.12 and 5.13 testpieces. Holds tend to be small pockets that can feel sharp. The canyon wall faces east, so it takes morning sun and shades over in the afternoon. A low cave to the left has boulder problems. A short uphill walk through boulders leads to the base.

nm_mid_town.blurb: The second of four sections of the shaded Shady Side crag near Alamogordo, found around the corner from the right end of the first section. Of its 22 routes, 21 are bolted sport lines and one is trad, running from the 5.8 range up to 5.13, with the bulk in the 5.11 and 5.12 bands and only a few easier warm-ups. The limestone here is steeper and shorter than the sunnier wall across the way, and the routes lean toward power rather than endurance. Shade makes it comfortable once the day in town reaches the mid 70s. The walk in is brief, with a climbers' trail and a short scree ledge.

nm_my_secret_garden.blurb: A traditional-only ridge of rock high in upper La Cueva Canyon on the west side of the Sandia Mountains above Albuquerque. The cliffs average about 170 feet, and every one of the roughly 20 routes needs a rack; none are bolted for protection. Grades run from about 5.6 up to 5.11, with the largest group at 5.11 and a good number of 5.8 to 5.10 lines in between, plus a couple of two-pitch climbs. Descents are by rappel from fixed anchors, and one 60 metre rope reaches the ground. The approach follows the La Luz Trail and crosses talus to the ridge, past the Fin.

nm_main_wall_upper_tier.blurb: The largest section of Pajarito Gorge, a basalt cliff on the edge of White Rock near Los Alamos. It has 21 routes, mostly trad and top-rope with a single sport line, running from the 5.8 range to the 5.12 range with most climbs at 5.10 and 5.11. The wall faces south, catching the sun most of the day, and the rim is windy. Climbs are exposed and fun rather than tall. Reaching the base takes thought, since the way down is a short stretch of exposed fourth-class scrambling; beginners and anyone carrying a pack may prefer to rappel instead.
nm_main_wall_upper_tier.parking_note: Drive into White Rock, turn south on Rover, go past Rover Park and turn right on Kimberly. Leave the car at the cul-de-sac at the end of the street.

nm_apache_canyon_a_k_a_grasshopper_canyo.blurb: A quiet, mostly shady bouldering canyon about twenty minutes from Santa Fe, with problems scattered along the creek and up the hillsides on either side. The centerpiece is a big overhanging sandstone block with many variations, and the circuit near it covers everything from very easy problems through the middle V grades to a few hard ones at the top end. Rock quality varies a lot, from good sandstone to crumbly stuff, and spring runoff can swamp low starts at the main boulder. Few climbers visit, though hikers are common. A short trail of about a quarter mile leads from the pull-off to the first boulders.
